text: Last lesson gave you the idea — combining systems multiplies dimensions. Now you compute the actual numbers: the Kronecker product formula that turns two small vectors or matrices into one larger one.

Given a vector A with m entries and a vector B with n entries, A tensor B is the length m times n vector built by taking every entry of A and multiplying it by the entire vector B, then stacking those results. Each piece is itself a block of n numbers, so the whole result has exactly m times n entries.

Take ket-zero equals 1,0 and ket-one equals 0,1. The first entry of ket-zero is 1, so the first block is 1 times ket-one, which is 0,1. The second entry is 0, so the second block is all zeros. Stacking gives 0,1,0,0 — and that matches the basis vector ket-zero-one exactly, the second slot. Tensoring in the opposite order, ket-one tensor ket-zero, gives 0,0,1,0 instead — a genuinely different vector.

The Pauli-X gate tensored with the identity describes 'flip qubit 1, leave qubit 2 completely alone,' acting on the combined 2-qubit space. Building it block by block from X's entries times the identity matrix gives a 4 by 4 matrix. Checking it: multiplying this matrix by the basis vector ket-zero-zero gives ket-one-zero — flip qubit 1 from 0 to 1, leave qubit 2's 0 untouched, exactly the intended action.

X tensor I and I tensor X are genuinely different 4 by 4 matrices — swapping the order of a tensor product is not the same operation, exactly the same way ket-zero tensor ket-one and ket-one tensor ket-zero are different vectors. Always keep track of which operand corresponds to which qubit.

Next lesson zooms out to what these tensor products build, collectively: the full state space a real multi-qubit quantum computer lives in, and why its size is the single biggest reason quantum computers are hard to simulate classically.
